intro: Twice in American history, a secret order called the Ku Klux Klan grew into a powerful force. The first Klan rode at night in the South after the Civil War. It used terror to keep freedpeople from voting, learning and owning land. The second Klan rose in 1915 and spread across the whole country, including Illinois. It sold memberships like a lodge and targeted Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants.

This unit puts the people who fought back at the center. You will meet survivors who testified to Congress, like the teacher and preacher Elias Hill. You will meet prosecutors, reporters, a Chicago league that printed Klan members' names, a young woman whose last words convicted a Klan leader, and Ida B. Wells, who fought lynching with facts from her home in Chicago.

By the end, you will be able to explain how secrecy helped a hate group escape the law. You will be able to compare sources that disagree and sort documented facts from disputed stories. You will also weigh a hard question: when does exposing names protect people, and when does keeping names private protect them instead?
bigQuestion: How did secrecy make the Klan powerful, and what finally broke its hold?

timeline.t: Six Confederate veterans form the Ku Klux in Pulaski, Tennessee.
Congress passes the Ku Klux Klan Act and forms the Joint Select Committee.
President Grant suspends habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties.
The committee's 13-volume report of testimony goes to Congress.
The White League forms openly in Louisiana to overturn Reconstruction.
Ida B. Wells publishes A Red Record in Chicago.
William J. Simmons launches a second Klan on Stone Mountain, Georgia.
The New York World begins its 21-day exposé of the Klan.
Chicago's American Unity League begins printing members' names in Tolerance.
A gunfight in a Herrin, Illinois, cigar store kills four men.
D. C. Stephenson is convicted of murder in Noblesville, Indiana.
NAACP v. Alabama protects the NAACP's membership lists.

words.d: the years 1865 to 1877, when the nation rebuilt the South and decided what freedom would mean
organized like an army but not an official army
violence and threats against ordinary people to reach a political goal
threats meant to make people too afraid to act
a person's right to be brought before a judge and not held in jail without cause
making people answer for what they do
the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing
a sworn statement by a person who knows he or she is dying, which a court may accept as evidence
the right to join together with others for a shared cause
a person's written account of his or her own life and experiences

test.q: Where and by whom was the first Ku Klux formed?
choices: In Pulaski, Tennessee, by six Confederate veterans
On Stone Mountain, Georgia, by William J. Simmons
In Chicago, by the American Unity League
In Nashville, by members of Congress
test.why: The first Klan began in Pulaski, Tennessee, as a club of six Confederate veterans. Simmons founded the second Klan in 1915.

test.q: What was the main goal of the first Klan's night riding?
choices: To raise money for veterans
To guard Southern towns from bandits
To keep Black citizens and their allies from voting and holding power
To enforce Prohibition
test.why: The first Klan used terror to stop Black citizens from voting, owning land, going to school and holding office.

test.q: Why is the Joint Select Committee's 1872 report so valuable to historians?
choices: It was written by Klan leaders
It holds the sworn testimony of hundreds of witnesses
It is a novel about Reconstruction
It lists every Klan member by name
test.why: Its 13 volumes hold sworn testimony from hundreds of witnesses, including survivors who named their attackers.

test.q: What did Elias Hill do that makes him central to this unit?
choices: He founded the White League
He wrote the Enforcement Acts
He directed The Birth of a Nation
He survived a Klan attack, testified, and led neighbors to Liberia
test.why: Hill, a disabled Baptist preacher and teacher, testified about the attack and led a group of neighbors to Arthington, Liberia.

test.q: Which part of the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 still matters today?
choices: Section 1, which lets people sue officials who violate their constitutional rights
The rule that set the Klan's joining fee
The rule that ended Reconstruction
The rule that created the NAACP
test.why: Section 1 survives as 42 U.S.C. section 1983, which the Supreme Court relied on in Monroe v. Pape, a Chicago police case.

test.q: How did the White League differ from the first Klan?
choices: It opposed white supremacy
It operated openly instead of in secret
It was founded in Illinois
It was a federal agency
test.why: The White League, founded in Louisiana in 1874, did not hide. It used violence openly.

test.q: What did The Birth of a Nation do in 1915?
choices: It exposed the Klan's crimes
It honored the witnesses of 1871
It glorified the first Klan and helped the second Klan recruit
It was banned everywhere before anyone saw it
test.why: The film showed the Klan as heroes, and Simmons used its fame to recruit for the new Klan.

test.q: How did the second Klan make money?
choices: Recruiters sold memberships for a $10 fee and kept a commission
It charged the government for protection
It sold newspapers
It won prize money from contests
test.why: Recruiters called Kleagles collected a $10 fee, kept a share and sent the rest up to leaders.

test.q: Which statement about where the 1920s Klan was strong is supported by the evidence?
choices: It existed only in the rural South
It never reached Illinois
It was strongest in New England
It was strong in Northern cities; Chicago had about 50,000 members
test.why: The Encyclopedia of Chicago counts about 50,000 members in the Chicago area, the largest city membership in the nation.

test.q: What was a surprising result of the New York World's 1921 exposé?
choices: Congress banned the Klan
Klan membership grew
Simmons went to prison
The World lost its readers
test.why: Klan leaders themselves said the exposé helped them grow. It was an unintended consequence.

test.q: What was the purpose of printing names in Tolerance?
choices: To recruit new Klan members
To sell advertising
To break the Klan's secrecy so members had to face their community
To protect members from harm
test.why: The American Unity League printed names so Klan members could no longer hide from their neighbors.

test.q: In the Williamson County Klan war, what do historians debate?
choices: Whether the raids were about liquor, prejudice against immigrants and Catholics, or both
Whether Herrin is in Illinois
Whether Prohibition existed
Whether the Klan ever held raids
test.why: The Klan said it was enforcing Prohibition, but many of those raided were Italian immigrants and Catholics, so historians see both motives.

test.q: What brought down D. C. Stephenson?
choices: A newspaper list of names
A Supreme Court ruling about the NAACP
A Superman radio show
Madge Oberholtzer's dying declaration, used as evidence at his murder trial
test.why: Her sworn statement was admitted in court, and he was convicted of second-degree murder in 1925.

test.q: Why did the Supreme Court protect the NAACP's membership list in 1958?
choices: The NAACP had broken no laws in any state
Revealing it would expose members to harm and weaken their freedom of association
The list had already been printed
Alabama asked the Court to protect it
test.why: In NAACP v. Alabama, the Court said forcing out the names would expose members to harm and weaken their freedom of association.

test.q: Which statement about Stetson Kennedy is best supported by the evidence?
choices: He invented the Klan
He had no part in fighting the Klan
He never wrote about his own role
He did real anti-Klan work, but much of his inside information came from an informant
test.why: The 2006 article Hoodwinked? reported the informant, while his defenders point to his real work against the Klan.

write.prompt: Which did more to break the Klan's power: witnesses who testified, laws and courts, or reporters who exposed it? Make a claim. Support it with two or three facts or sources from this unit, and explain why they matter.
tips: Name your sources, such as the 1872 committee report, the Ku Klux Klan Act or the New York World series.
Use unit words like testimony, accountability and exposé correctly.
Give the other side fairly before you explain why your claim is stronger.
Keep the survivors and witnesses at the center of your answer.
